a: The Köppen climate classification, developed by German climatologist Wladimir Köppen in 1884 and later refined with Rudolf Geiger, is the most widely used system for categorizing world climates based on native vegetation, temperature, and precipitation patterns. The system divides climates into five principal groups symbolized by letters: A (tropical), B (dry), C (temperate), D (continental), and E (polar), with a separate category H (highland) often added for mountainous regions. Each main group is further subdivided using additional letters—for example, Af (tropical rainforest), Aw (tropical savanna), BWh (hot desert), Csa (Mediterranean), Dfb (humid continental with warm summer), and ET (tundra)—allowing for precise classification of local climates based on seasonal patterns of temperature and rainfall.

q: What are tropical climates like?

a: Tropical climates (Köppen group A) are defined by average temperatures above 18°C (64°F) every month, with no winter season, and are found in a broad belt around the equator between approximately 25° north and south latitude. Tropical rainforest climates (Af) receive at least 60mm of precipitation every month—often exceeding 2,000mm annually—supporting tall, dense, multi-layered evergreen forests with immense biodiversity, as seen in the Amazon Basin, Congo Basin, and Indonesian archipelago. Tropical monsoon climates (Am) have a short dry season and a very wet rainy season driven by monsoonal wind shifts (e.g., Mumbai, Yangon), while tropical savanna climates (Aw/As) feature distinct wet and dry seasons with annual rainfall between 500-1,500mm, supporting fire-adapted grasslands with scattered trees, typical of the African Serengeti, Brazilian Cerrado, and Indian Deccan plateau.

a: Dry climates (Köppen group B) are characterized by annual precipitation that is less than potential evaporation, divided into arid (desert, BW) and semi-arid (steppe, BS) subtypes, each further separated by temperature into hot (h) or cold (k) varieties. Hot deserts (BWh) like the Sahara, Arabian, and Kalahari experience extreme heat with summer temperatures exceeding 50°C and annual rainfall below 250mm, while cold deserts (BWk) like the Gobi and Great Basin have hot summers but bitterly cold winters. Semi-arid regions (BSh/BSk) receive 250-500mm of rainfall annually and support drought-resistant grasses and shrubs, forming transitional zones between deserts and more humid climates, with ecosystems ranging from North American shortgrass prairies to African Sahel and Australian outback shrublands.

q: What are temperate and continental climates?

a: Temperate climates (Köppen group C) have mild winters and warm to hot summers, with average temperatures of the coldest month between -3°C and 18°C, and include Mediterranean climates (Csa/Csb) with dry summers and mild, wet winters ideal for citrus and olive cultivation, humid subtropical climates (Cfa/Cwa) with hot, humid summers and mild winters supporting deciduous and coniferous forests, and oceanic climates (Cfb/Cfc) with cool summers and mild, rainy winters prevailing in coastal Western Europe. Continental climates (Köppen group D) have severe winters with average temperatures below -3°C in the coldest month and warm to hot summers, found in interior regions of North America, Europe, and Asia, supporting boreal forests (taiga) in their colder variants. These climates shape distinct biomes—from the Mediterranean maquis shrublands and Southeast Asian subtropical forests to the vast coniferous and mixed forests of Canada, Scandinavia, and Siberia.
